title: The Anarchist Cookbook: Funny but Dangerous
summary: Josh and Chuck examine The Anarchist Cookbook, a 1971 book compiled by 19-year-old William Powell, covering its contents (drug recipes, weapons and sabotage instructions), Powell's background and the New York anti-war context, its publisher Lyle Stewart, FBI and media reaction, its use in real-world violent crimes including the 1976 Croatian hijacking and Grand Central bomb, Powell's later regret and attempts to suppress it, and its continued circulation online. The episode closes with a listener mail segment about band names and album titles.

segments.title: Opening
segments.summary: Josh introduces the show and the episode topic, a discussion of The Anarchist Cookbook.

segments.title: Reputation and contents of the book
segments.summary: The hosts describe The Anarchist Cookbook (1971) as a book containing drug recipes, weapons instructions and bomb-making, note its use as evidence in court cases, and say much of its content was copied from available sources, including an LSD recipe taken from an Eli Lilly patent.

segments.title: Real-world crimes linked to the book
segments.summary: Chuck lists people who owned the book, including Timothy McVeigh, Thomas Spinks, and the Boston Marathon bombers, and notes the author was an angry 19-year-old who later repudiated it.

segments.title: William Powell's background
segments.summary: Powell was born in the US, raised partly in England, bullied for his accent, expelled from boarding school, moved to New York at 17, and avoided Vietnam draft with a 4F classification. He roomed with anarchist Steve Hancock, who inspired the project.

segments.title: Origins and anti-war context
segments.summary: Powell worked at a bookstore where he met Valerie Solanas, and the hosts describe the anti-war militancy of New York in 1967-68 and Powell's aim of spreading revolutionary information.

segments.title: Powell's writing, drawings and dubious claims
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the book's forward claiming it is for the silent majority, Powell presenting himself as an expert despite lacking experience, his amateurish drawings such as a garrote illustration, and invented statistics about hand-to-hand combat.

segments.title: Weapons and drug recipes
segments.summary: The hosts list the book's contents, including LSD, mushrooms, converting shotguns to grenade launchers, silencers, and killing with piano wire, and recall friends' copies. They discuss hoax drug recipes like banana peel smoking and nutmeg.

segments.title: Tone, warnings and the cookbook label
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the book's warnings against drug misuse, its dramatic writing style at age 19, and the fact that many recipes are drug-related rather than cooking.

segments.title: Publication and Lyle Stewart's promotion
segments.summary: Powell's manuscript was rejected by thirty publishers before Lyle Stewart published it unchanged. Stewart promoted it with a press conference that was disrupted by a smoke bomb.

segments.title: FBI and media reaction
segments.summary: The FBI questioned Powell's parents and colleagues but not Powell himself. Media ran alarmist headlines, and the FBI concluded the book was protected under the First Amendment.

segments.title: Ad break transition
segments.summary: Short transition between segments before the discussion of the book in the wrong hands.

segments.title: 1976 Croatian hijacking and Grand Central bomb
segments.summary: In 1976 Croatian separatists hijacked a New York to Chicago flight and demanded their manifesto be printed. A bomb at Grand Central Station killed officer Brian Murray, and the hijackers said they got bomb information from the book. Powell had by then become religious, left for Alaska and special education work, and had no copyright over the book, which Lyle Stewart owned.

segments.title: Out of print period and Powell's later life
segments.summary: Powell earned royalties, was forced out as head of an international school in Tanzania after parents objected, and the book went out of print for about eleven years after a publisher bought the rights. Powell later returned to lead the school.

segments.title: Powell's regret and continued circulation
segments.summary: Powell publicly disavowed the book and asked Amazon to post a statement, but Lyle Stewart reclaimed and reprinted it. Counterfeit editions and PDFs remain online. Powell died in 2016.

segments.title: Lessons for young writers
segments.summary: The hosts reflect on being bold while considering long-term consequences of what one publishes, especially calls for violence.

segments.title: Listener mail: missed band names
segments.summary: A listener named AR suggests band names and album titles the hosts missed in an earlier episode on love drugs, and the hosts invite more submissions.
